items.title: Dan Carney Has Died. He Co-Founded Pizza Hut and Then Made It Ubiquitous.
items.summary: The franchise with the iconic red roof began small, in a tiny brick hut in Kansas. Little more than a decade later, it was the world’s biggest pizza chain. He was 95.
items.full_text:
Title: Dan Carney Has Died. He Co-Founded Pizza Hut and Then Made It Ubiquitous. - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/26/business/dan-carney-dead.html

Published Time: Thu, 26 Nov 2026 19:40:29 GMT

Markdown Content:
Dan Carney, who founded Pizza Hut with his brother Frank, transforming a single location in Wichita, Kan., into one of the most recognizable restaurant chains in the world, thanks to ambitious franchising and a distinctive red roof, died on Nov. 13 at his home in Wichita. He was 95.

The cause of death, his son Michael said, was chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

The Carney brothers, who were of Irish descent, became pizza kings by happenstance. In 1958, Dan was 26 and running his family’s corner grocery, Carney’s Food Market, when the owner of a tiny brick building nearby came in with a copy of The Saturday Evening Post and a proposal.

She wanted to oust her tenant, a tavern that sold burgers and beer, and showed Mr. Carney an article in the magazine about a new culinary trend.

Image

The first Pizza Hut opened in Wichita, Kan., in 1958, and it “was, in fact, a hut,” Mr. Carney said.Credit...Wichita State University

Image

Mr. Carney, left, with his brother Frank in an undated photo of the original Pizza Hut.Credit...via Carney Family

“She said, ‘How would you like to go into the pizza business?’” he recalled in an interview for the 2025 documentary “[Slice of Life: The American Dream. In Former Pizza Huts](https://sliceoflifedoc.com/).” “And I said, ‘Yeah, OK.’ We knew nothing.”

He brought in Frank, who was then 19 and attending the University of Wichita (now Wichita State University), and they borrowed $600 from their mother to open the restaurant. They found their first pizza chef through their sister Sally: Her neighbor, an airman named John Bender, had worked at a pizzeria in Indiana. Mr. Bender, who developed Pizza Hut’s early sauce recipe, became the third partner. (Several years later, he sold his share of the business to the brothers.)

That first restaurant, at the intersection of Bluff and Kellogg Streets, was around 500 square feet. (The building is [now a museum](https://www.wichita.edu/museums/pizzahutmuseum/history.php) on the campus of Wichita State.) Dan’s wife Beverly made the curtains and tablecloths. The pizza ingredients came straight from Carney’s Food Market. And the pizza oven was found discarded behind an Italian restaurant.

Image

Mr. Carney, left, with his brother Frank, center, and Robert Chisholm, the company’s treasurer, in 1966, celebrating the sale of the chain’s 14 millionth pizza.Credit...via Carney Collection, via Wichita State University

Despite its humble beginnings, Pizza Hut was an immediate success, in part thanks to the Carneys’ community ties, but also because of the novelty of a Neapolitan dish in a meat-and-potatoes Midwestern city. They opened five restaurants in just over a year.

Within a few years, as the brothers sold franchises, Pizza Huts spread — from Kansas to surrounding states, including Missouri, Oklahoma, Colorado and Nebraska, and eventually across the United States and as far as away as Australia and China.

The story of Pizza Hut is not about that first successful restaurant, but about the second one, and the third and the fourth, and so on, Jay Price, a professor of history at Wichita State, said. The brothers were early adopters of the franchise model, Dr. Price said in an interview: “The idea of having another one, another one, another one. The food is consistent; the service is consistent.”

Frank, the more outgoing brother, was the front-of-the-house guy and unofficial spokesman, while Dan preferred the back-of-the-house role dealing with logistics, contracts and other details related to business growth.

It was Dan who gave the American landscape the two-tiered red roof — as iconic a piece of roadside architecture as the golden arches of McDonald’s.

Image

Mr. Carney, right, and his brother Frank in the 1970s with their instantly recognizable building — encircled by windows shaped like pizza slices and topped with a two-tiered roof.Credit...Pizza Hut

The first Pizza Huts were a hodgepodge of architectural styles based on available space. But by the early 1960s, Dan recognized the need for a branded building that would set Pizza Hut apart from competitors like Shakey’s Pizza.

He hired an architect, and the resulting design — a red roof topped by a cupola, with unusual trapezoidal windows below, said to have been inspired by the shape of pizza slices — was “conspicuous, noticeable and standardized,” Philip Langdon, an architecture and design writer for The Atlantic, [told The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/07/movies/pizza-hut-architecture-documentary.html).

It was also enduring. Forty years later, that design had become the architectural equivalent of comfort food.

“People walk into these buildings and straightaway know it’s a Pizza Hut,” said Matthew Salleh, who co-directed “Slice of Life,” about the repurposing of former Pizza Hut buildings to house other businesses, including churches and marijuana dispensaries. “What an amazing achievement of design to make a building that owns a common shape.”

Michael Daniel Carney was born on Oct. 6, 1931, in Kansas City, Mo., one of seven children of Mary Frances (Compton) Carney and Michael Carney, a meatpacker who opened a grocery store in Wichita.

When he was a teenager, his father died and he stepped in to run the business. At some point, Mr. Carney’s son Michael said, he reversed the order of his first and middle names, becoming Daniel Michael Carney.

Image

An early work schedule for Pizza Hut, showing how the brothers and their co-workers divvied up duties.Credit...Wichita State University

After graduating from the University of Wichita in 1953 with a degree in business administration, Mr. Carney spent two years in the Air Force. During his downtime, he studied the concept of franchising. His eventual ambition, [he told the “All Things Pizza” podcast](https://podcasts.apple.com/ca/podcast/episode-11-untold-stories-from-the-founder-of-pizza-hut/id1437666983?i=1000528133207&l=fr-CA) in 2021, “was to put as many Pizza Huts in as I could.”

By the mid-60s, there were 145 Pizza Huts across the country. By 1971, Pizza Hut had become the world’s largest pizza chain, with some 1,000 restaurants around the world.

Mr. Carney prized personal relationships and favored handshake deals, and the business had in some ways outgrown his skill set and capital: Going global requires corporate structure and marketing power. In 1977, he and his brother sold the company to PepsiCo for $300 million (the equivalent of about $1.7 billion today).

Frank stayed on with the company until 1980, and then tried various other business ventures that mostly failed, losing millions. Later on, much to Dan’s dismay, Frank became the owner of a Papa Johns franchise and appeared in a commercial for the rival chain. He [died](https://www.nytimes.com/2020/12/04/business/frank-carney-dead.html) in 2020 at 82.

Dan went from founder to franchisee, for a time owning Pizza Huts in Florida and Mexico. As a prominent business and civic leader in Kansas, he also served on charitable boards and backed younger entrepreneurs.

Image

Mr. Carney and his first wife, Beverly, in an undated family photo.Credit...via Carney Family

Mr. Carney married Beverly Singleton in 1954. She died in 1998. He married Gayla Coulter in 2001. In addition to his son Michael, she survives him, along with another son, Matthew; three daughters, Karen Carney, Tricia Kaufman and Polly Vickers; 15 grandchildren; and 22 great-grandchildren. A fourth daughter, Kay Carney, died in 2008.

In recent years, Pizza Hut has struggled to attract customers. In June, a private-equity firm [bought](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/16/business/pizza-hut-yum-brands-sold.html) the restaurants in the United States and around the world, except those in mainland China, which were sold to another company.

Nevertheless, generations of diners remember the chain fondly as a destination for family nights out, where bonding took place over breadsticks and deep-dish pan pizza. The affection is such that the locations that retain their original red roofs and familiar décor have become a [popular draw](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/03/03/dining/pizza-hut.html).

Throughout his life, Mr. Carney remained humble about his business achievement. It was the right time and the right place, and they had a good product, he told interviewers.

On coming up with the name, he told the “Slice of Life” filmmakers, “The little hut we had was, in fact, a hut. So it didn’t take big brains to call it Pizza Hut.”

items.title: Democrats Confront a Familiar Question: How Are You Going to Pay for That?
items.summary: Many Democratic plans are unlikely to become law under President Trump. But the party is still grappling with the difficult budget math of its agenda.
items.full_text:
Title: Democrats Confront a Familiar Question: How Are You Going to Pay for That? - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/26/business/democrats-congress-agenda-taxes-spending.html

Published Time: Thu, 26 Nov 2026 20:34:13 GMT

Markdown Content:
Democrats have made no secret of the agenda they plan to pursue when they control the House and Senate next year. Reversing President Trump’s cuts to the social safety net, reining in his tariffs and restoring health insurance subsidies are all primed for votes in the opening days, if not hours, of the new Congress.

Largely left unsaid is if — or how — they’ll pay for those plans.

As long as Mr. Trump remains in the White House, many Democratic proposals are unlikely to become law and, therefore, would not have any actual effect on the budget. Nevertheless, Democrats are starting to confront the difficult math of both unraveling Mr. Trump’s policies and pursuing a proactive agenda of their own. The deliberations are an early window into the fiscal challenge the party will face if it wins total control of Washington in 2028.

Democrats have had to puzzle together a way to finance their agenda after past election victories. But the nation’s fiscal situation is much more challenging now. Mr. Trump’s tax cuts piled on to a federal deficit that has remained much larger than it was before the coronavirus pandemic. Interest rates have also stayed elevated, fueling investors’ fears that the government’s debt load could, in the not-so-distant future, make it more expensive for Americans to borrow money.

“It’s a really big hole they’re inheriting,” said Ben Ritz, a budget analyst at the Progressive Policy Institute, a center-left think tank. “Whatever Democrats do today sets the stage for the next time they have a trifecta, which could be in two years.”

Many Democrats support the idea of raising taxes on companies and the wealthy, and Democratic lawmakers and their aides have been dusting off revenue plans in preparation for next year. But translating populist, tax-the-rich talk into policy changes that become law has been a challenge for the party. In California this month, [voters rejected](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/09/us/california-billionaire-tax-prop-40.html) what would have been the first wealth tax in the nation, a [blow to the progressive tax agenda](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/business/billionaire-tax-progressive-agenda.html).

Democrats’ ambitions are also large enough that the tax increases that may already be palatable to many in the party, like modestly raising the income tax rates on corporations and high-earning individuals, would likely not pay for the full scope of their plans.

Image

Mr. Trump’s tax cuts, which he signed into law in July 2025, added significantly to the federal deficit, which has remained larger since the coronavirus pandemic.Credit...Tierney L. Cross/The New York Times

Just rolling back the parts of Mr. Trump’s agenda that Democrats spent the election campaigning against could cost more than $4 trillion over a decade, according to an estimate from the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, which pushes for a smaller deficit. More sweeping changes Democrats are considering, like an expansion of Medicare or a more generous child tax credit, could add trillions more.

“We should be exploring those sorts of things, and I think that we have to remind the American people: Are you willing to pay for them?” said Representative Richard E. Neal of Massachusetts, the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Committee, which writes tax legislation. “Many of those items can be and are pricey.”

Those potential costs are set to renew a debate among Democrats about whether the national debt is an urgent problem and how far to go in raising taxes. Historically, the party’s centrist members have been both the most concerned about the country’s fiscal situation and the most hesitant to support substantially raising taxes. Progressives, on the other hand, see raising taxes on the rich as a political asset but chafe against letting bean counters dictate the party’s agenda.

A potential wild card is how the party’s new lawmakers, especially those elected from historically red districts and states, approach budget questions. For instance, Annie Andrews, the South Carolina Democrat elected to the Senate, included a pledge to cut taxes in her campaign platform alongside support for a constitutional amendment requiring a balanced budget.

There are also tactical considerations about how to use control of Congress under divided government. Some in the party believe that going through the process of drafting tax increases could help Democrats seem more substantive, all while preparing them for their next potential turn in power. But including tax increases would reduce the likelihood that any Republicans support the legislation. And others in the party worry that fiscal considerations could overcomplicate straightforward votes on bills that are meant to unify Democrats — and that won’t likely become law, anyway.

Image

Annie Andrews, a South Carolina Democrat, was elected to the Senate after pledging to cut taxes in her campaign platform.Credit...Win Mcnamee/Getty Images

“Democrats ran on addressing the cost-of-living crisis that is affecting ordinary Americans, and they should not hold back on those proposals out of a manufactured fear of debt,” said Kitty Richards, a senior fellow at the Groundwork Collaborative, a progressive group that favors higher taxes on the rich.

The conversations could start to come to a head in the coming weeks. Some House Democrats have started organizing an effort to impose a House rule requiring that the cost of legislation brought to the floor be covered by tax increases or other spending cuts. The rule, called “pay as you go” or PAYGO, would not apply to all spending, and versions of the rule adopted by previous House Democratic majorities have been easy to waive. But whether the rule is adopted will be an early indicator of how Democrats approach their fiscal dilemma.

“We just have to have this conversation,” said Representative Scott Peters, a California Democrat who is among those pushing for the inclusion of the rule. “PAYGO forces us to go in that room and have that conversation like adults.”

Much of the fiscal challenge for Democrats stems from the tax cut Republicans passed last year. The G.O.P. tried to offset the cost of those tax cuts with steep cuts to health care and food stamp programs. But the law still cost more than $4 trillion over a decade. Democrats have so far rallied around repealing those spending reductions, though doing so is expensive enough that some in the party are exploring the possibility of preserving some elements of the Republican spending changes. One option is to leave in place limits Republicans put on [Medicaid provider taxes](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/05/06/upshot/medicaid-hospitals-republicans-cuts.html?eafs_enabled=false) while rolling back other cuts the G.O.P. made to the program.

Image

Democrats ran on addressing the cost-of-living crisis that is affecting ordinary Americans.Credit...James Estrin/The New York Times

Mr. Trump’s tax cuts are a different question. Democrats may be able to easily reverse some of them, including by raising the top marginal individual income rate, which is now at 37 percent. But many of the Republican-passed tax cuts, like an expanded standard deduction, provide benefits to working-class Americans that Democrats are unlikely to want to claw back since such moves would amount to de facto tax increases. Even some of the law’s provisions that primarily benefited the rich, like a larger deduction for state and local taxes, enjoy Democratic support.

The new majority party will also be forced to grapple with Mr. Trump’s campaign promises to not tax tips, overtime or Social Security. When Republicans turned those catchphrases into law, they did so only temporarily, setting them up to expire at the end of 2028. Many Democrats have supported the tax breaks, which are largely targeted to middle-class Americans. One of the few areas of potential bipartisan compromise next Congress may be a deal between Democrats and Mr. Trump to extend those tax cuts, which could cost more than $400 billion over a decade.

Democrats would likely be able to attract Republican support for such a deal, meaning it would be able to pass the Senate easily. But bills repealing Mr. Trump’s cuts to Medicaid, canceling his tariffs or expanding Obamacare subsidies would face hurdles. Even though they won a 56-seat majority in that chamber, Democrats are still short of the 60 votes needed to overcome a filibuster for most legislation.

That means Democrats [may resort](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/us/politics/house-democrats-affordability-costs-budget.html?eafs_enabled=false) to a special budget process, called reconciliation, to pass tax and spending legislation. Reconciliation allows lawmakers to avoid the 60-vote threshold in the Senate, but it also includes a number of fiscal rules, including that long-term changes to the budget be paid for. Those rules would require Democrats to come up with enough tax increases to cover the long-term cost of their agenda, even for a bill that Mr. Trump would veto. That procedural requirement may ultimately shape how they proceed.

“I expect any of this stuff to eventually be paid for, regardless,” said Bobby Kogan, a budget analyst at the Center for American Progress, a liberal think tank.
